questions.q: Why is a password alone considered a weak form of identity proof?
options: Passwords are always too short to be secure
A password is "something you know," which can be stolen via phishing, breach, or keylogging without the user doing anything else wrong
ServiceNow cannot store passwords securely
Passwords expire automatically after one use
questions.explain: The core weakness is that a password is a single piece of knowledge that can be captured and reused by an attacker who never needed physical access to anything.

questions.q: What does MFA add that a strong password by itself cannot provide?
options: A faster login experience
A second, independent proof of identity — typically something the user physically has, like a device generating a one-time code
A replacement for the IdP entirely
Automatic password resets every 30 days
questions.explain: MFA requires a second factor from a different category of proof — something you have — rather than relying solely on something you know.

questions.q: Where do most enterprises actually enforce MFA, according to this lesson?
options: Natively inside ServiceNow's own login page
At the Identity Provider, the same system already handling SAML-based SSO
Nowhere — MFA is rarely used in enterprise environments
Inside the sys_user table directly
questions.explain: Enforcing MFA at the IdP applies it consistently across every connected application through the same authentication chokepoint, rather than configuring it separately per application.

questions.q: In the seven-step SAML login flow, at which step does IdP-enforced MFA actually take effect?
options: Step 6, when ServiceNow validates the assertion's signature
Step 3, when the user authenticates at the IdP
Step 1, when the user first navigates to ServiceNow
MFA never maps onto the SAML flow at all
questions.explain: MFA inserts itself into the authentication step at the IdP — the user must satisfy the password and the second factor there before the IdP issues the signed assertion.

questions.q: A user reports an MFA failure. Per this lesson's guidance, what's the most likely place to check first?
options: The sys_security_acl table in ServiceNow
The IdP side of the flow — a lost device, expired code, or unapproved push notification
ServiceNow's field-level ACLs
The user's role assignments in sys_user_has_role
questions.explain: Since MFA enforcement typically lives at the IdP, an MFA failure is usually an IdP-side issue rather than a ServiceNow configuration problem.
